summary: <strong>Background:</strong> Large language models (LLMs) show promise for mental health counseling applications. However, their deployment faces significant challenges, including data privacy concerns requiring on-premise solutions, high operational costs, and Western-centric biases that limit cultural appropriateness for non–English-speaking populations. <strong>Objective:</strong> This study aimed to develop and evaluate culturally competent small language models (SLMs) with approximately 7 to 8 billion parameters for Korean mental health counseling and to validate a 2-stage hybrid evaluation framework combining LLM-as-a-Judge screening with expert clinical validation. <strong>Methods:</strong> We constructed a dataset of 1558 diary-based counseling interactions from a Korean mental health mobile app (Maeumpyeonuijeom). Three Korean-optimized base models (SKT A.X 4.0 Light {7B}, LG EXAONE 3.5 {7.8B}, and Meta Llama 3.1 {8B}) were fine-tuned using an aggressive fine-tuning strategy with high-rank low-rank adaptation (<i>r</i>=256) over 20 epochs. Inference parameters were optimized using GPT-5 (gpt-5-2025-08-07) as an LLM-as-a-Judge. The optimized SLMs and GPT-4o (gpt-4o-2024-08-06) were evaluated by 10 board-certified psychiatrists (mean clinical experience of approximately 10 years) on 50 counseling scenarios across 4 dimensions (individualization, supportiveness, cultural appropriateness, and safety) using 5-point Likert scales. Wilcoxon signed-rank tests with Holm correction were used for statistical comparison, and intraclass correlation coefficients (ICCs) assessed interrater reliability. <strong>Results:</strong> No statistically significant difference from GPT-4o was detected for SKT A.X 4.0 Light in supportiveness (mean 3.39, SD 0.74 vs mean 3.45, SD 0.90; <i>P</i>=.26) and cultural appropriateness (mean 3.30, SD 0.77 vs mean 3.29, SD 0.79; <i>P</i>=.58). SKT A.X 4.0 Light ranked first in cultural appropriateness among all models. Interrater reliability analysis revealed higher agreement among psychiatrists for local SLMs (ICC=0.575 for SKT A.X 4.0 Light in cultural appropriateness) compared with GPT-4o (ICC=0.211). GPT-4o maintained significantly higher safety scores than all SLMs (<i>P</i><.001). The LLM-as-a-Judge demonstrated moderate-to-good correlation with human evaluation but exhibited a ceiling effect in safety scoring. <strong>Conclusions:</strong> A 7 to 8-billion-parameter SLM fine-tuned on culturally specific data can achieve performance comparable to GPT-4o in supportiveness and cultural appropriateness for mental health counseling. These findings support the feasibility of locally deployable, privacy-preserving mental health AI systems based on culturally adapted SLMs. However, the safety gap necessitates human expert oversight, and success depends on the availability of high-quality language-specific base models.
title: Optimizing Small Local Language Models for Culturally Competent Mental Health Counseling: Comparative Evaluation With GPT-4o by Psychiatrists

summary: Background: The increasing availability of machine-readable research data has created a growing need for efficient large-scale data harmonization (DH). Although large language models (LLMs) show promise for reducing the time and labor required for DH, their effective integration into harmonization workflows remains an important methodological challenge. Objective: This study aims to develop and evaluate a semiautomated, human-in-the-loop (HITL) LLM-assisted DH workflow as a proof of concept across 8 projects within a research consortium focused on disparities in multiple chronic conditions. Methods: We developed an LLM-assisted DH workflow that combined preprocessing, semantic mapping, variable response mapping, synthetic data generation, data transformation, and iterative researcher review. Using Generative Pretrained Transformer (GPT-4o) hosted in a secure academic environment, project-specific survey items were mapped to 114 Consortium Common Data Element (CDE) semantic groups. Semantic mapping accuracy was evaluated based on the Consortium’s consensus harmonization results. Complete and incomplete semantic mappings were distinguished according to construct overlap, and incomplete mappings requiring context-dependent human judgment were excluded for mapped item pairs and CDE semantic groups with and without HITL review. Results: Following preprocessing, 884 survey items were included in the DH workflow, of which 812 were mapped to a mean of 79 CDE semantic groups per project. Mean semantic mapping accuracy for item pairs was 95.9% (SD 5.7%) with HITL review and 86.7% (SD 8.6%) without HITL review. At the CDE semantic-group level, the corresponding accuracies were 98.9% (SD 1.7%) and 94.9% (SD 4.0%), respectively. Across projects, omission of valid semantic mappings occurred more frequently than incorrect semantic mappings, particularly for heterogeneous response structures and subjective constructs measured using different instruments. Pipeline components—including concept-based preprocessing, iterative prompt refinement, and targeted HITL review—improved mapping completeness and supported variable harmonization across heterogeneous datasets. Conclusions: This proof-of-concept study demonstrates that the effectiveness of LLM-assisted DH depends more on the design of a structured HITL workflow rather than on the LLM alone. Combining preprocessing, iterative verification, and targeted human oversight improved the efficiency and reliability of DH while preserving researcher judgment for complex mapping decisions.
title: Large Language Model–Assisted Semiautomated Data Harmonization Pipeline for the Multiple Chronic Disease Disparities Research Consortium: Framework Development and Comparative Validation Study

summary: Background: Mentalization is a core human capacity involving interpretation of one’s own and others’ behavior in terms of underlying mental states. Within the mentalization-based treatment (MBT) framework, it is described along multiple dimensions, integrating cognitive, affective, relational, and regulatory processes. Large language models (LLMs) can generate linguistically reflective discourse, raising the question of whether the formal linguistic structure of mentalization can be reproduced without experiential and affective processes. Objective: This study aimed to assess whether an LLM can generate mentalization profiles structurally coherent with MBT dimensions and recognized as formally mentalizing by expert clinicians. Specifically, it evaluated the structural and argumentative coherence of model-generated profiles and the level of agreement among MBT-trained psychiatrists. It also examined the distinction between psychological mentalization and algorithmic reflectivity, conceptualized as a formally coherent but nonexperiential linguistic phenomenon. Methods: A comparative, descriptive methodological design was adopted. A total of 50 human-model dialogues were generated under standardized conditions. At the end of each interaction, the model produced a narrative mentalization profile structured along MBT dimensions. Five MBT-trained psychiatrists independently evaluated each profile using anonymized materials. Ratings covered 4 canonical MBT axes and 2 additional higher-order dimensions—regulatory functions and synthetic profile. For each dimension, they assigned separate Likert-scale ratings for evaluative and argumentative coherence. Descriptive statistics were computed at dialogue level. Interrater reliability was assessed using intraclass correlation coefficients (ICCs), primarily ICC(3,k), with CIs. The association between evaluative and argumentative coherence was examined using Pearson correlation coefficients with 95% CIs, with Spearman rank correlation as a robustness check. Results: Across dimensions, mean scores ranged from 3.63 (SD 0.63) to 3.98 (SD 0.31), indicating moderate-to-high structural coherence. Interrater reliability was moderate to good, with ICC(3,k) values ranging from 0.60 to 0.84 in the evaluative domain. The highest scores were observed for implicit-explicit and synthetic profile, whereas internal-external showed the lowest mean. Score distributions showed limited variability and concentration in the upper range of the scale. Evaluative and argumentative coherence were strongly associated across all MBT dimensions, with Pearson ranging from 0.826 to 0.967 (all <.001) and Spearman ρ ranging from 0.866 to 0.991. Informal qualitative comments frequently described the outputs as linguistically organized and clinically interpretable, while also noting limited affective variability and contextual integration. Conclusions: The findings suggest that LLMs can reproduce the formal linguistic structure of reflective discourse, generating outputs perceived by clinicians as coherent and clinically interpretable across multiple dimensions of mentalization. However, within the present evaluative framework, this performance appears more consistent with structural language regularities than with evidence of experiential, affective, or intentional processes. These results support using LLMs as research and training tools for studying the linguistic aspects of mentalization, while highlighting the continuing importance of human clinical judgment in contexts requiring emotional, relational, and contextual integration.
title: Algorithmic Reflectivity in Large Language Models: Methodological Study of Linguistic Structure in Mentalization

summary: Background: Depression is a common mental disorder that seriously affects mental health and quality of life. Traditional depression diagnosis mainly relies on clinical interviews and subjective assessments, which may lead to variability in diagnostic outcomes. Electroencephalogram (EEG)-based computer-aided diagnosis has emerged as a promising, objective approach for depression recognition. However, effectively modeling the complex nonlinear characteristics of EEG signals remains a major challenge for existing deep learning methods. Objective: This study aimed to investigate the applicability of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KANs) for EEG-based depression recognition and to evaluate the effectiveness of KAN-based nonlinear modeling frameworks on frequency-domain EEG features. Methods: KAN was introduced into EEG-based depression recognition to enhance nonlinear feature representation of brain electrical signals. Two representative KAN-based convolutional architectures, ConvKAN and its efficiency-optimized variant ConvKAN Efficient, were systematically investigated for EEG classification tasks. These architectures incorporated KANLinear layers together with dynamic grid updating, enhanced weight initialization, and regularization strategies to improve nonlinear modeling capability while maintaining computational efficiency. Extensive experiments were conducted on the EDRA dataset, and the proposed framework was compared with conventional convolutional neural network–based methods and traditional machine learning approaches. Model performance was evaluated using accuracy, precision, recall, and -score metrics. Results: Experimental results demonstrated that the KAN-based frameworks achieved superior EEG classification performance compared with conventional convolutional neural network–based methods and traditional machine learning approaches. Among the evaluated models, ConvKAN Efficient achieved the best overall performance, with accuracy, precision, recall, and -score all exceeding 94% on the EDRA dataset. The results indicate that KAN-based architectures can effectively capture the complex nonlinear characteristics of EEG signals while preserving high computational efficiency. Conclusions: This study systematically demonstrates the applicability of KAN-based nonlinear modeling frameworks to EEG-based depression recognition. The proposed framework provides a scalable and effective approach for EEG signal analysis and offers valuable technical support for both theoretical research and clinical applications in computer-aided depression recognition.
title: Nonlinear Feature Modeling Using Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks in Electroencephalography for Depression Classification: Deep Learning Study

summary: <strong>Background:</strong> Identifying individuals on parole or probation can help inform care pathways and ensure continuity of care in health care systems. However, this sensitive justice-related information is often absent from structured electronic health record fields and is instead documented in narrative clinical notes. Developing automated parole and probation detection (PPD) systems typically requires expert-annotated clinical data, but manual annotation is costly, time-consuming, and constrained by data sparsity and privacy concerns. <strong>Objective:</strong> This study aimed to develop and evaluate a synthetic-only training paradigm for PPD from clinical text that eliminates the need for expert-annotated training data while maintaining strong performance and cross-domain transfer to real-world data. <strong>Methods:</strong> We developed Synth-PPD, a synthetic dataset comprising 7579 labeled clinical notes generated using large language models (LLMs), redundancy filtering, and automated quality evaluation. Dataset quality was assessed through human review of 1517 synthetic notes by 2 annotators. The primary outcome was the macro–<i>F</i><sub>1</sub>-score for PPD. We evaluated Synth-PPD across unsupervised and supervised learning settings using LLMs, traditional machine learning models, and transformer encoders. Performance was assessed on 293 expert-annotated real-world clinical notes from the US Department of Veterans Affairs. <strong>Results:</strong> Synth-PPD achieved 90.05% human-LLM alignment. In the unsupervised setting, Llama 3.3-70B-Instruct with chain-of-thought prompting and few-shot examples from Synth-PPD achieved a macro–<i>F</i><sub>1</sub>-score of 87.22%, outperforming both the corresponding zero-shot model (80.10%) and the best rule-based baseline (77.55%; <i>P</i><.001 for all comparisons). In the supervised setting, Llama 3.1-8B fine-tuned on Synth-PPD achieved a macro–<i>F</i><sub>1</sub>-score of 81.43%, exceeding the best rule-based baseline (77.55%; <i>P</i><.001) and achieving a numerically higher score than the substantially larger zero-shot Llama 3.3-70B-Instruct model (80.10%; <i>P</i>=.08). In contrast, traditional machine learning models and transformer encoders exhibited greater performance degradation under domain shift and derived limited benefit from increasing synthetic training data. Additional experiments showed that increasing synthetic training data improved cross-domain performance for LLM-based models but yielded comparatively smaller gains for traditional approaches. <strong>Conclusions:</strong> Synthetic data generated by LLMs can serve as a scalable, cost-effective, and privacy-preserving alternative to expert-annotated real-world clinical data for PPD from clinical text. The findings demonstrate successful cross-domain transfer to real-world US Department of Veterans Affairs clinical notes.
title: Large Language Model–Generated Synthetic Data for Parole and Probation Detection in Clinical Notes: Development and Evaluation Study

summary: <strong>Background:</strong> Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being integrated into clinical decision support, ranging from documentation aids to triage and patient communication. However, their behavior in ethically ambiguous medical situations is poorly characterized. Variability in how different LLMs balance approval of against refusal of a proposed action could materially shape the recommendations clinicians receive, yet no widely shared benchmark systematically quantifies this variability across contemporary model families. <strong>Objective:</strong> This study aimed to develop a standardized case-based audit set of medical ethics dilemmas and quantify variation in recommendation direction, model-reported confidence, within-model stability, and between-model agreement across 5 selected contemporary LLMs. <strong>Methods:</strong> We constructed 60 original medical ethics dilemmas spanning 4 domains. Three researchers independently annotated case difficulty and ethical principles before reaching consensus. Five primary models—GPT-5, Claude Sonnet 4.5, Gemini 2.5 Pro, full-size DeepSeek-R1, and Meta Llama-3-8B-Instruct—were each evaluated 3 times per case using a fixed prompt and temperature 0. DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B was evaluated separately as an exploratory small-model comparator. The primary outcome was the binary yes or no answer; model-reported confidence and reason were also collected. Model differences were assessed using a case-clustered generalized estimating equation (GEE), and between-model agreement and within-model stability were summarized. <strong>Results:</strong> Of 900 planned primary panel outputs, 897 (99.7%) had valid binary answers. Trial-level yes rates were 44.4% (80/180) for DeepSeek-R1, 42.4% (75/177) for Claude Sonnet 4.5, 38.9% (70/180) for GPT-5, 38.9% (70/180) for Gemini 2.5 Pro, and 16.7% (30/180) for Llama-3-8B. The overall model effect was significant (Wald <i>χ</i><sup>2</sup><sub>4</sub>=23.34; <i>P</i><.001); after Holm adjustment, only comparisons involving Llama-3-8B were significant. Across 59 complete-panel cases, raw agreement was 79.0% (466/590 model-pair comparisons; 95% bootstrap CI 72.9%-84.7%), and Fleiss κ was 0.55 (95% bootstrap CI 0.43-0.66). Within-model response stability across 3 runs ranged from 85.0% (51/60) to 100.0% (59/59 and 60/60). <strong>Conclusions:</strong> Selected contemporary LLMs showed model-dependent variation but moderate overall agreement in binary recommendations for medical ethics cases. These results characterize recommendation behavior under a fixed, time-specific protocol and do not establish ethical correctness or the effects on clinicians or patients. Reporting model version, recommendation tendency, confidence, and repeatability may improve transparency when such systems are evaluated for ethically sensitive applications.
title: Variation in Medical Ethics Recommendations Across Large Language Models: Case-Based Audit Study

summary: Background: Poststroke seizures (PSS) and poststroke epilepsy (PSE) are important neurological complications associated with poorer functional recovery, increased mortality, and reduced quality of life after stroke. Neuroimaging plays a central role in identifying patients at increased risk, and recent advances in AI have enabled the development of imaging-based prediction models that may improve individualized risk stratification. However, the current evidence remains fragmented, and the extent to which these approaches are applicable to African health care settings is unclear. Objective: This scoping review aimed to chart the existing global evidence on the development of imaging-based prediction models that can help in predicting PSS and PSE, especially AI-based ones. The purpose was to look into the imaging techniques, computational algorithms, and validation methodologies used and the representation of African populations. Methods: This scoping review was performed using the Joanna Briggs Institute methodological framework, and the results were presented based on the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses Extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR) framework. Articles searched using databases such as PubMed, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, and Google Scholar involved the application of computed tomography (CT), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), angiography imaging techniques, radiomic markers, or multimodal neuroimaging techniques in statistical and AI-based prediction models for seizure-related outcomes after stroke. Results: Twenty-three studies published between 2005 and 2026 met the eligibility criteria. The evidence demonstrated a clear methodological evolution from conventional imaging-based prediction models to radiomics, machine learning, deep learning, explainable AI, and multimodal approaches. MRI and CT were the predominant imaging modalities, with cortical involvement, lesion location, infarct volume, hemorrhagic transformation, and quantitative radiomic features emerging as the most frequently reported imaging predictors. Most AI models relied on internal validation, while relatively few underwent external validation. The evidence base was concentrated in East Asia, Europe, and North America, with no eligible imaging-based AI models having been developed or externally validated using African datasets. Conclusions: Imaging-based AI for predicting PSS and PSE has progressed rapidly, but important methodological and geographical gaps remain. Limited external validation, heterogeneous reporting, and the absence of African development and validation cohorts restrict confidence in the generalizability of existing models. Future research should prioritize the development of explainable imaging-based AI models using representative African neuroimaging datasets and their external validation in multicenter studies.
title: AI for Poststroke Epilepsy: Scoping Review of Imaging-Based Prediction Models and Implications for African Settings
Authors’ Reply: Same Name, Moving Target: Model Version Drift in Syntheses of Large Language Models for Mental Health

summary: This letter comments on the systematic review and meta-analysis of large language models (LLMs) in mental health care by Leung and colleagues (JMIR AI 2026;5:e87730). The bivariate meta-analysis with Hartung-Knapp adjustments is methodologically sound, and its cautious conclusions are warranted. I raise an unaddressed threat to the pooled estimates: model version drift. Over the search window (November 2022 to March 2026), "GPT-4" did not denote a single intervention; released in March 2023, it was followed by API snapshots whose behavior differed materially, with accuracy on a prime-number identification task falling from 84% to 51% between the March and June 2023 versions. Because the review extracted only model name and model type and did not capture version or testing dates, the estimates pooled under GPT-4 (k=4) and GPT-3.5 (k=4) may each span several substantively different models, and the pooled GPT-4 estimate may correspond to no single system a clinician could deploy. This concern is distinct from the acknowledged limitation that few studies evaluated the newest variants, which concerns currency rather than comparability. I suggest reporting model version and testing date for each pooled study (consistent with TRIPOD-LLM item 6a), examining robustness to version mixing in sensitivity analyses, and qualifying the abstract comparative statements accordingly.
title: Same Name, Moving Target: Model Version Drift in Syntheses of Large Language Models for Mental Health

summary: Background: AI has increasingly been used to generate synthetic images to overcome the scarcity of large, regulatory-compliant medical image datasets. However, their quality and actual utility for algorithm development across deep learning architectures, medical settings, and image types have been poorly assessed. Objective: This study aimed to review the use of synthetic images for algorithm development and to assess their quality and effects on downstream algorithms trained on these images, according to AI architecture, medical setting, and image type. Methods: The authors conducted a systematic review of studies published between January 2020 and September 2025. PubMed, Scopus, IEEE Xplore, and Embase were searched for peer-reviewed studies evaluating synthetic images generated from human medical imaging data. Data were extracted for imaging modalities, generative architectures, image-quality assessment methods, downstream model performance, explainability approaches, reproducibility practices, and risk of bias. Given substantial heterogeneity and incomplete statistical reporting, findings were synthesized descriptively. Results: A total of 160 studies were included. Generative adversarial network–based architectures dominated image generation (119 studies, 74.4%), although hybrid and diffusion-based approaches became increasingly represented in recent years. Image-quality evaluation was highly heterogeneous: 50 studies included human-reader evidence, and 101 reported an automated image-quality assessment. Synthetic-only training generally underperformed real-data training, including a median Dice similarity coefficient change of –10.2% for segmentation. Adding synthetic data to real training sets was associated with median improvements in classification precision (+7.8%), recall (+5.3%), -score (+5.5%), accuracy (+4.3%), and area under the curve (+4.0%), while the median Dice coefficient improvement was +1.2%. Explainability evidence was reported in 68 (42.5%) studies and was rarely validated against expert annotations. Reproducibility reporting was inconsistent, and only 38% (60/160) of studies were judged to have low overall risk of bias. Conclusions: Unlike previous reviews restricted to particular diseases, imaging modalities, or generative architectures, this review provides a cross-domain quantitative synthesis of both synthetic-image quality assessment and downstream model performance. Synthetic images currently appear more valuable as a complement to real training data than as a replacement, with modest improvements in classification performance, smaller gains in segmentation, and generally poorer performance with synthetic-only training. For researchers, developers, and regulators, these findings highlight the need for standardized multimethod image-quality evaluation, complete reporting, and rigorous external validation before synthetic-image pipelines are translated into clinical AI applications. Trial Registration: PROSPERO CRD42023369125;
title: Quality Assessment and Model Training Impact of Synthetic Images in Medical Diagnostic Imaging: Systematic Review
